centralObject.ref: Petition for a writ of certiorari, Mahmoud Khalil (counsel incl. Baher Azmy, Center for Constitutional Rights), filed in the U.S. Supreme Court 2026-10-19, seeking review of the Third Circuit panel ruling of 2026-01-15 (rehearing en banc denied 6–5, 2026-05-22; mandate stayed pending review); the Court has not acted
centralObject.name: Mahmoud Khalil's petition asking the Supreme Court to let a federal district court hear his speech-retaliation claim by habeas corpus

place.why: Cert grants are rare and the removal order is already moving in the Fifth Circuit, but a cited circuit split, a 6-5 en banc denial and a self-stay give the petition a real if minority chance of drawing a federal judge onto the speech claim.

tethers.statute: Immigration and Nationality Act — judicial-review channeling ("zipper clause")
tethers.title: Judicial review of orders of removal — consolidation of questions for judicial review
tethers.enacted: 1952 (INA); §242 rewritten by IIRIRA 1996; amended by the REAL ID Act 2005
tethers.why: The provision that sends questions 'arising from' removal into the petition-for-review track, which the Third Circuit read as barring his district-court habeas claim. Coverage in the window names the INA generally; the subsection is Claude's identification.

place.why: As read by the Third Circuit it is delivering in force: his claim is in the immigration track and the Fifth Circuit. Claude's place.

tethers.cite: 28 U.S.C. §2241; U.S. Const. art. I, §9, cl. 2 (Suspension Clause)
tethers.title: Power to grant writ
tethers.why: The route the petition asks the Court to open: a district court hearing his detention claim directly. The Suspension Clause is where the en banc dissent's 'constitutional rights' argument lands. Claude's identification.

place.why: For this petitioner the writ is currently closed by the channeling ruling; it delivers only if the Court grants and reverses. Claude's place.

tethers.statute: Immigration and Nationality Act — foreign-policy deportation ground
tethers.title: Deportable alien — foreign policy
tethers.enacted: 1952 (INA); the foreign-policy ground added by the Immigration Act of 1990
tethers.why: The ground Secretary Rubio's determination rests on ('compromise a compelling U.S. foreign policy interest'); the petition does not attack it directly, but it is the power whose use against speech the retaliation claim would test. Same provision as the Sarsour draft (rdg_zjxak4ltqrk7).

place.why: It has produced a removal order upheld by the BIA, so it is delivering for the government; its speech limit is untested in this case. Claude's place.

title: Which Judge
prompt: Khalil asks the Supreme Court to let a federal judge hear his free-speech claim before he can be deported. Does the petition get him that hearing?
framing: On Monday, October 19, 2026, Mahmoud Khalil, the former Columbia graduate student and pro-Palestinian activist arrested by immigration agents in March 2025, asked the Supreme Court to hear his case. He wants to overturn a Third Circuit ruling of January 15, 2026, which held that the Immigration and Nationality Act requires him to bring his claim that he was detained in retaliation for his speech through immigration proceedings, not to a federal district court through habeas corpus; the full court declined to rehear it 6–5 on May 22, 2026. Khalil, a green-card holder, has not been charged with a crime. His lawyer Baher Azmy called the case an “unprecedented weaponization of immigration power.” A White House spokeswoman said, “Those who lie to the government to obtain entry into the United States will face justice.”

split.seam: Whether the circuit split and the 6-5 en banc vote make a grant plausible: left-institutional reads the docket signals as live, while the other three stations read the odds and the Fifth Circuit clock as closing the door, for opposite reasons.
split.rationale: Delivery belief is mostly negative across the plane; the fight is over whether that outcome is the statute working (right) or the courts abandoning speech (left populist), with left-institutional the only station betting on the grant.

zPattern.note: Centers are fluid z; coalition z: A -0.1, B -0.35, C -0.3, D -0.2. Object's own z -0.4.

antiValentRationale: In the coalition band every station holds its read of the petition while worrying that its own side has turned the case into a symbol or a power it will regret, which is where the four voices sound most alike.

z.pos: the petition delivers: the Court takes it and a federal judge hears whether the government detained and is deporting him for his speech, before he can be removed
z.neg: it doesn't: the Court declines or affirms, the claim stays inside the immigration system, and he can be removed before any federal judge rules on his speech

fluid.zReason: A cited circuit split, a 6-5 en banc denial with a three-judge dissent, and the Third Circuit staying its own ruling are the standard markers that raise cert odds above the base rate.

instrument.holder: the Supreme Court, asked by Khalil's petition to resolve a clean circuit split

fluid.text: Look at the record: a circuit split on when immigrants can get into federal court, an en banc vote that went 6-5, and the Third Circuit staying its own ruling so he could ask. That's exactly the kind of petition the Court grants. If it does, a district judge finally gets to ask whether he was locked up for what he said.
words: an en banc vote that went 6-5
locked up for what he said

coalition.zReason: The jurisdiction argument is strong, but grants are rare and a symbolic framing gives the Court no reason to reach a politically charged case it can deny without comment.
coalition.text: I still think the petition is strong on the jurisdiction question, and I'd file it the same way. But the people I march with already talk about him like a verdict on the whole Court, and I can hear it hardening. If the case becomes a loyalty test, a denial will read as proof of something instead of what it is, a thin docket decision.

denominated.zReason: Reads the Court as aligned with executive power, so it expects a denial that leaves the claim inside the immigration system.

instrument.holder: a Supreme Court that defers to the executive

denominated.text: This Court lets the executive jail dissidents and calls it channeling.

fluid.zReason: Section 1252(b)(9) channels removal-related claims to the petition-for-review track, and the claim already has an Article III forum pending in the Fifth Circuit, so the Court has little reason to grant.

instrument.holder: Congress's INA review scheme, applied by the Supreme Court

fluid.text: Congress wrote the zipper clause so that every challenge arising from removal runs through the immigration courts and then the court of appeals, and that's where his claim is right now, in the Fifth Circuit. He isn't being denied a judge; he's being told which judge. I don't see four votes to grant on that.

coalition.zReason: Still expects the statute to hold, but concedes a split plus an aggressive foreign-policy ground is the kind of question that can attract four votes.

instrument.holder: the Supreme Court reading the INA

coalition.text: The statute reads the way the Third Circuit read it, and I'd defend that ruling anywhere. What bothers me is how many people I vote with have stopped arguing the INA and started cheering the deportation itself. If the case gets argued as payback for campus protests, the next administration will use the same foreign-policy ground on someone they don't like.
words: statute reads the way the Third Circuit read it

denominated.zReason: Treats the visa-misrepresentation allegation as dispositive, so the petition is a stunt that the Court will turn away.
denominated.text: Activists who lie on visa forms don't get a constitutional stage.

fluid.zReason: Cert is granted in roughly one case in a hundred while the removal order is already upheld, so the Fifth Circuit can finish him before the justices ever act.
fluid.text: A cert petition is a long shot for anybody, and this Court takes maybe one in a hundred. Meanwhile the removal order's already upheld and the Fifth Circuit can move faster than the justices. So what's the petition actually buy him, a hearing or just time?

coalition.zReason: Supports the filing as the last open route but expects the odds to stay low, and sees the movement's framing pre-writing a loss.
coalition.text: I'll back the petition because it's the only door left open. But the crowd I rally with already wrote the ending, and every sign with his face on it turns a legal question into a symbol. If he's deported, half of them will say it proves the courts were never real, and I'm not sure that helps the next student who gets picked up.
words: the next student who gets picked up

denominated.zReason: Sees the courts as part of the state that is deporting him, so no petition can deliver a real hearing.
denominated.text: Say Palestine and the empire deports you, courts or no courts.

fluid.zReason: Reads removal as an ordinary immigration matter that the statute routes to immigration court, and expects the Court to refuse a celebrity exception.
fluid.text: He's not a citizen, he's in removal proceedings, and the law says you fight removal in immigration court. That's the process every other green-card holder gets. The Supreme Court isn't going to carve out a special lane because he's famous.
words: a special lane because he's famous

coalition.zReason: Expects denial but sees that a one-signature foreign-policy determination against a lawful resident is the kind of executive reach a court might want to check.

instrument.holder: the Supreme Court and the executive

coalition.text: I want the immigration laws enforced, and I think the Court leaves this one alone. Still, the folks I'm around online want him gone so badly they've stopped asking what else this power reaches. A secretary of state signs a paper saying your activities hurt foreign policy, and that's it? I'd want a judge to look at that if it were someone on my side.

denominated.zReason: Treats him as an enemy to be removed, so the petition is noise that changes nothing.
denominated.text: Pro-Hamas agitators get a plane ticket, not a hearing.

LF.text: The petition puts one question in front of the justices: can the government jail a green-card holder for his speech and keep every federal judge out of it?

LC.text: I'm all in on the petition, but the people I organize with keep treating a cert filing like a referendum, and I worry they won't hear the answer if it's no.

LD.text: It was never about a visa; it's a regime punishing Palestine.

RF.text: The INA sends his claim through immigration court and then the Fifth Circuit, and the petition asks the justices to rewrite that because the case is loud.

RC.text: I think the petition fails on the statute, but the people I vote with are cheering a deportation instead of defending a law, and that's a habit that comes back around.

RD.text: Liars and agitators get deported, and that's the whole story.

objectLayer.stated: A cert petition asking whether the INA's channeling provisions bar a green-card holder from bringing a speech-retaliation detention claim in federal district court by habeas corpus.
objectLayer.operative: Whether the executive can use the foreign-policy deportation ground against a lawful resident for pro-Palestinian speech and remove him before any federal judge rules on the retaliation claim.
objectLayer.inversion: Right-institutional voices that usually defend judicial review against executive overreach here defend channeling claims away from district courts, a lean rather than a settled reversal.
